items.stem: After two consecutive losses a trader doubles position size to 'win it back fast'. What behaviour is this?

options.text: Revenge trading driven by the urge to recover losses
options.rationale: Correct: increasing size to recoup losses emotionally is classic revenge trading.
It abandons the plan in response to emotion, the opposite of discipline.
Sizing up after losses increases risk rather than controlling it.
There is no hedge; it is an emotional escalation of risk.

items.explanation: Correct: increasing size to recoup losses emotionally is classic revenge trading.

items.stem: Which TWO habits most directly support trading discipline? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Following a written pre-market checklist before trading
options.rationale: Correct: checklists reduce impulsive, emotion-driven decisions.

options.text: Setting a rule to stop trading after a defined daily loss
options.rationale: Correct: a hard stop-loss limit protects against tilt.

options.text: Increasing size whenever a trade feels certain
options.rationale: Acting on a feeling of certainty invites overconfidence bias.

options.text: Avoiding any journaling so losses are not dwelt on
options.rationale: Skipping journaling removes the feedback that builds discipline.

items.explanation: Correct: checklists reduce impulsive, emotion-driven decisions.

items.stem: A trader only reads news that agrees with an open long position and ignores bearish signals. Which bias is this?

options.rationale: Correct: seeking only confirming information while ignoring disconfirming evidence is confirmation bias.
Recency bias is over-weighting the most recent events, not filtering by agreement.
Anchoring is fixating on a reference number, not selective reading.
Survivorship bias concerns ignoring failures in a sample, not one-sided news reading.

items.explanation: Correct: seeking only confirming information while ignoring disconfirming evidence is confirmation bias.
